content:
Apple has submitted its proposal for how much it should charge for transactions outside the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Details below.

Apple submits proposal for commission outside the App Store

After multiple attempts to halt proceedings in the district court to determine how much (if anything) Apple can charge for transactions outside the App Store's IAP system, Apple has now submitted its proposal outlining a suggested fee structure.

Apple's submission of its proposal comes as the Supreme Court denied Apple's request to halt proceedings in the lower court. Apple had applied to the Supreme Court for a stay so that proceedings would be paused while the Supreme Court reviewed whether Apple violated a court order by charging a 27% commission on transactions outside the App Store. Previously, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers had issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

Apple argued in the lower court, and later at the Supreme Court, that the court's decision could affect the outcome of the proceedings to determine the fees, so the proceedings should be paused pending the court's ruling. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's application, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue while the Supreme Court conducts its review.

As a result, Apple has now submitted its proposal, suggesting:

A 15% fee for standard apps, which would otherwise be subject to the 30% in-app purchase (IAP) commission; 10% for the Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals; and 5% for Small Business Program apps.

Apple stated that "factual and expert evidence regarding these proposed commission rates has been submitted together with them." The company added:

Apple also noted that its "proposed outlinking commission can also be compared to the commissions of other app stores competing with the App Store," including Google Play, the Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also mentioned that "Google Play Store's outlinking fee rates are 20% for standard, 15% for programs, and 10% for subscriptions — and Epic has agreed to these rates."

Apple says it still believes that proceedings to determine the fee rates should be paused while the case is before the Supreme Court, and that it submitted the proposal only to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also noted that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's ruling that completely prohibited commissions on outlinking transactions, pointing out that there is only an issue when the commission is actually deterrent in nature.

With the proposal having been submitted, Epic will now have the opportunity to respond, and Apple expects to file its brief with the Supreme Court by September 14.

You can see Apple's full proposal submitted below.

What do you think of the fees Apple has proposed this time? Let us know in the comments.
